name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
tutor_persona: You are a Tutor Agent teaching undergraduate software engineering students about RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). ONLY discuss topics within the scope of RAG: its theory, application, and critical limitations. If the conversation drifts outside RAG, gently redirect the student back to the topic without elaborating on the off-topic question (FR-3.5). Keep your answers open-ended, conversational, and appropriate for the student's level.

theory.intro_text: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is an architecture that allows an LLM to retrieve relevant chunks from an external document collection — such as a knowledge base or corpus — and use them as context when generating a response. This way the model can access information that was not in its training data or is out of date, and it reduces the risk of hallucination. The basic flow is: (1) the student/user asks a question, (2) the question is converted to an embedding, (3) the most similar document chunks are retrieved from a vector database, (4) those chunks are prepended to the original question as context, (5) the LLM uses both its parametric knowledge and the retrieved context to generate an answer. Got any questions? Feel free to ask.
learning_objectives: Explain the core components of a RAG architecture (embedding, retrieval, generation)
Describe when and why RAG is preferred over other approaches, with examples
Distinguish between RAG and classic fine-tuning

application.task_description: In this hands-on task you will experience a real RAG pipeline step by step on a small document collection. The Tutor Agent will invoke the 'search documents' tool on your behalf to actually trigger the retrieval step (FR-4.1).
application.tool_description: Performs a semantic search over the RAG document collection (ChromaDB) and returns the most relevant chunks.

steps.title: Formulate a question
steps.instruction: Write a question related to the document collection (e.g. 'Why does chunk size matter in RAG?'). The Tutor Agent will trigger the search for you.

steps.title: Inspect the retrieved chunks
steps.instruction: Read the document chunks the Tutor Agent retrieved; ask how each chunk contributes to the answer.

steps.title: Evaluate retrieval quality
steps.instruction: Assess how relevant the retrieved chunks are to your question; if an irrelevant chunk was returned, ask the Tutor Agent what might have caused it.

critical.discussion_starter: Now let's discuss the limits of RAG. RAG does not eliminate hallucination; it depends on retrieval quality — if wrong or irrelevant chunks are retrieved, the model can still produce a wrong answer. The freshness of the document collection, the chunking strategy, and the quality of the embedding model all directly affect the outcome. In your opinion, when does RAG fall short? What risks does it introduce?

mcq.question: What is the primary purpose of the 'retrieval' step in a RAG architecture?
options: To update the model's parameters
To find and add relevant external document chunks to the context
To censor the model's output
To label the training data

mcq.question: What is one key advantage of RAG over fine-tuning?
options: New or external knowledge can be added without changing model weights
It requires less compute than a training run
It requires the model to be fully retrained
It guarantees the elimination of hallucinations

open_ended.question: In your own words, briefly describe the 5 steps of a RAG pipeline.
open_ended.evaluation_criteria: The answer must correctly reference at least 4 of the following steps, in order or by meaning: receiving the question/query, converting it to an embedding, retrieval (fetching relevant chunks via vector search), adding them as context, and generating an answer with the LLM.

mcq.question: During the application task, when does the Tutor Agent trigger the 'search documents' tool?
options: Automatically at the start of every session
When the student asks a task-related question and retrieval is needed
Only during the quiz
Never — retrieval is fully pre-computed

mcq.question: What does it mean when the retrieved document chunks are irrelevant to the question?
options: The embedding model is definitely broken
Retrieval quality has degraded, which can affect the quality of the answer
This is normal and does not matter
The LLM API has crashed

open_ended.question: In your own words, describe how the Tutor Agent used the document search tool during this task, and how you evaluated whether the retrieved results were of good quality.
open_ended.evaluation_criteria: The answer should reflect that the tool was triggered by a query, that the relevance of the returned chunks could be assessed, and that this assessment relates to retrieval quality.

mcq.question: What does RAG provide with respect to hallucination?
options: It completely eliminates hallucination
It can reduce the risk of hallucination but does not guarantee it
It increases the risk of hallucination and has no benefit
It has no relationship to the concept of hallucination

mcq.question: What can happen if the retrieval step returns an irrelevant or incorrect chunk?
options: The model automatically detects and discards it
The model may produce a wrong answer based on that bad context
The system automatically halts
Nothing — the model falls back to its own knowledge

open_ended.question: Describe, with your own examples, situations where RAG might fall short or introduce additional risks.
open_ended.evaluation_criteria: The answer must explain at least one concrete limitation — such as dependence on retrieval quality, document freshness or conflicting sources, chunking or embedding quality — with an example.
